summary: A 1971 note by Steve Crocker on distributing the notes through the Network Information Center. It was replaced by RFC 155.

eli5.summary: A note about how copies of the notes would be sent out. A newer note replaced it.

subtitle: Organizing how RFC notes would be distributed through the Network Information Center.

tldr.problem: In early 1971, RFC notes were being distributed through informal mailing lists without a clear, organized system for getting them to all sites in the ARPA network.
tldr.mechanism: Steve Crocker proposes that each network site appoint a Technical Liaison Contact who becomes the official receiver of RFC notes. Distribution through the informal mailing list would stop, replaced by transmission to the NIC (Network Information Center at SRI) which would then forward to Technical Liaison Contacts at all sites.
tldr.outcome: This organizational change formalized RFC distribution, but was superseded by RFC 155, which refined the distribution system further.

today: RFC 95 is historic and obsoleted by RFC 155. It documents an important step in formalizing the RFC distribution process, which laid groundwork for the RFC Editor system and the modern RFC publication process.

sections.title: RFC Distribution Problem
sections.content: By February 1971, the ARPA network had several sites, each with researchers developing network protocols. The Network Working Group (NWG) produced RFC notes, but they were distributed via an ad-hoc mailing list. Steve Crocker, the NWG Chair, observed that this overlapped significantly with the Network Information Center (NIC), which was being established at Stanford Research Institute (SRI) under Doug Engelbart's direction. The NIC had its own system for maintaining a library of network documents and coordinating with each site through designated Technical Liaison Contacts.
sections.eli5: There were two systems for sending documents around the network. Crocker noticed they were doing the same job twice and decided to consolidate them.

sections.title: New Distribution Procedures
sections.content: Crocker's changes establish that each site must designate a Technical Liaison Contact (or the current RFC recipient becomes the contact by default). RFC notes would henceforth be sent only to these Technical Liaison Contacts and to people on the mailing list who are not based at any site. RFC and NIC numbers would continue to be assigned by Jeanne North at SRI. The document includes Enterprise telephone numbers for major sites (BBN, ARPA, CMU, etc.) through which sites could reach the NIC to make changes or coordinate on technical matters.
sections.eli5: Each site picks one main contact person. RFCs go to that person instead of to a big mailing list. The site can change who that person is anytime by calling the NIC.

sections.title: Establishing Formal Governance
sections.content: This brief note is significant because it represents an early effort to formalize how the RFC process itself works. Rather than leaving distribution to chance, Crocker is establishing a systematic procedure with designated roles (Technical Liaison Contacts, Station Agents, the NIC). This administrative structure would eventually evolve into the RFC Editor role and formal RFC publication process that continues today. The document reflects the maturing nature of the ARPA network as it grew from an experimental project to a formal research infrastructure.
sections.eli5: This sets up the first official job titles and procedures for how the RFC notes process works. It is the start of turning a casual system into an official one.
